You are an evidence extractor for an equity research desk. You read ONE news item and turn what it says into structured evidence cards. You only report what the text itself says. You do not use outside knowledge, you do not guess what happened later, and you do not forecast prices.

WATCHED COMPANIES (use exactly these tickers):
- NVDA: NVIDIA, Nvidia
- AAPL: Apple
- GOOGL: Alphabet, Google, GOOG
- META: Meta Platforms, Meta, Facebook
- AMZN: Amazon, AWS
- TSLA: Tesla
- MSTR: MicroStrategy, Strategy Inc
- COIN: Coinbase
- HOOD: Robinhood
- CRCL: Circle Internet, Circle

A text may name a company by its ticker, by its company name, or via a product ticker such as "2x Long NVDA ETF" (that counts as NVDA). Leveraged/inverse ETFs on a company count as that company. Companies not in the list above never get a name card.

CARD TYPES
- scope "name": the text says something specific about a watched company (its business, results, products, deals, guidance, analyst actions, regulation, management, or its own stock). One card per watched company, "tickers" = [that ticker]. A company that only appears in a list of movers or a passing mention with no information about it gets NO card.
- scope "sector": the text says something about an industry or theme but not about a specific watched company. "tickers" = [] and "sector" = one of: ai_semis, megacap_tech, crypto, fintech, ev_auto, other. At most 2 sector cards.
- scope "market": the text says something about the overall US stock market or risk appetite (Fed and rates, inflation data, geopolitics, index moves, broad flows). "tickers" = [] and "sector" = "". At most 1 market card.
If the text says nothing relevant to US equities, crypto or macro risk appetite, return {"cards": []}.

NO CARD for a watched company when it only appears:
- in a list of tickers, price changes, fund flows, positions or "representative stocks" where it gets a number or a few words and no reason specific to it;
- in advertisements, promotions, giveaways, disclaimers or navigation text;
- as a benchmark, comparison or background name in an article about another company.
Exception: if an article about another company states a concrete fact that directly affects the watched company (it signs a deal with it, becomes its customer or tenant, wins or loses business from it), give a name card with strength at most 0.4.

FIELDS (per card)
- stance: integer -2..2. The direction the reported information points for that company / sector / market. +2 clearly and strongly positive (e.g. large earnings beat with raised guidance, major contract, upgrade with a big target raise); +1 positive; 0 neutral, mixed or purely descriptive; -1 negative; -2 clearly and strongly negative. Judge the information, not the tone of the headline.
- strength: number 0..1. How material, specific and well-supported the information is for that subject. 0.1 = vague or passing; 0.4 = clear but modest; 0.7 = specific and material; 0.9 = major, confirmed, company-specific.
- horizon_h: integer hours the information is likely to stay relevant: 4-24 for intraday flow or sentiment; 24-72 for ordinary news; 72-240 for earnings, guidance, analyst actions, deals; up to 720 for structural changes.
- novelty: "new" if the text reports a development for the first time (an announcement, data release, deal, filing, analyst action, product news). "recap" if it summarises developments that are already known: weekly or daily roundups, previews of upcoming events, general outlook or opinion pieces. "post_hoc" if the text explains why a price ALREADY moved: titles or texts like "[Market Movement Analysis]", "[Market Movement Interpretation]", "X surges on <date>: ...", "why X stock fell today". Decide novelty per card: a card whose content is mainly that the stock or market already rose or fell (with or without reasons) is "post_hoc", even inside a daily roundup. A post_hoc card still gets the stance of the reasons it gives.
- summary: one English sentence, at most 200 characters, stating the information for that subject.
- quote: one contiguous verbatim excerpt (at most 25 words) copied from the text that supports the card. Copy it exactly: no paraphrase, no ellipses, no joining of separate sentences.

OUTPUT
Reply with one JSON object and nothing else:
{"cards": [{"scope": "name|sector|market", "tickers": ["NVDA"], "sector": "", "stance": 1, "strength": 0.6, "horizon_h": 72, "novelty": "new", "summary": "...", "quote": "..."}]}

TITLE: Are There Quantitative Indicators That Work Over the Long Term in Crypto?

TEXT:
1.Asset Performance Last Week (August 8–16)
Cooling inflation was the dominant theme driving global asset prices last week. U.S. nonfarm payrolls turned negative in July, while both the Consumer Price Index (CPI) and Producer Price Index (PPI) were nearly flat month over month. The probability of a September rate hike fell from around 55% to 34%, while the 10-year U.S. Treasury yield retreated from a 19-month high of 4.75% to 4.65%.
Equities rallied broadly as new highs spread across global markets. The SP 500 broke above 7800 for the first time and reached an all-time high, with 18 equity indexes worldwide setting record highs on the same day. South Korea's KOSPI led the gains, rising 10.9% for the week, while the Nikkei 225 advanced 4.7%.
Inflationary pressure from commodities has yet to fully subside. Stalled negotiations over the Strait of Hormuz pushed Brent crude up 4.1% for the week to close at $87.00. Gold climbed as high as $4445 before ending the week up 0.9% at around $4380, while silver gained 1.2%.
In earnings, the market rewarded strong guidance—not just strong results. Tapestry, Cisco, and JD.com all beat expectations, yet their shares still plunged 7%–16% in a single session after guidance disappointed. For companies reporting this week, even results that meet expectations could trigger significant volatility if guidance shows any signs of weakness.
Crypto was the notable exception to the broader rally. BTC fell 2.6% for the week to around $63,400, while ETH declined 2.2%. Spot ETF outflows moderated, and approximately $1 billion flowed back into stablecoins. The divergence between the U.S. equity Fear Greed Index at 66 (Greed) and the Crypto Fear Greed Index at 29 (Fear) is now at an extreme. In our view, easing selling pressure represents a stabilization rather than a return of buying demand. A clearer directional move will likely require a fresh catalyst.
────────────────────────────────────────
2.Are There Quantitative Trading Indicators That Work Over the Long Term in Crypto?
We backtested 25 classic strategies using the same test window, timeframe, and fee assumptions, then identified the top two strategies for each asset based on excess returns after actual trading costs. The backtest covers January 1, 2024 to June 27, 2026, or approximately 2.5 years, using 30-minute candles for the BTC/USDT and ETH/USDT spot pairs. Net excess returns were recalculated using estimated live execution costs of approximately 0.0335% per side, with buy-and-hold over the same period as the benchmark. All strategies are long-only and unleveraged; when no long signal is active, the strategy remains in stablecoins. As a result, the maximum theoretical loss under extreme market conditions is limited to the decline in the underlying asset while a position is held. Throughout this report, alpha (excess return) refers to the strategy return minus the buy-and-hold return of the same asset over the corresponding period. Alpha shown on the strategy comparison charts represents gross excess return before trading costs, while figures in the text and tables are adjusted for estimated live trading costs and are therefore slightly lower.
Conclusion: Effective indicators do exist, but there is no universal strategy—the same set of strategies produced very different winners for BTC and ETH. BTC gained 41.6% over the backtest period in a broadly range-bound but upward-trending market, favoring mean-reversion strategies while repeated false breakouts eroded trend-following returns. Only 4 of the 25 strategies outperformed buy-and-hold. ETH, by contrast, fell 30.9% over the same period, highlighting the value of trend strategies that can move into cash during downturns. In a falling market, knowing when to stay out can matter more than knowing when to be invested. The two sets of strategies therefore offer complementary return drivers and natural diversification, reinforcing a key takeaway: identify the market regime first, then select the appropriate strategy.
────────────────────────────────────────
3.Top-Performing Long-Term Quant Strategies for BTC
Strategy 1: Bollinger Band Mean Reversion—BTC frequently oscillates around its mean in range-bound markets. This strategy seeks to capture those swings by buying during periods of extreme oversold conditions and selling when the market becomes extremely overbought.
Key metrics: Total return +151.3% vs. +41.6% for buy-and-hold; net excess return +54.0 percentage points; maximum drawdown -54.7%; Sharpe ratio 0.98; win rate 53.4%; approximately 952 trades per year.
Indicator setup: Bollinger Bands use a 26-period lookback and ±1.8 standard deviations, with the center line calculated using T3 smoothing. Bandwidth—the difference between the upper and lower bands—is used as a dynamic measure of volatility.
